questions.question_text: Before preparing a project presentation, the first thing a presenter should establish is the:
options: Font to be used on the title slide
Colour scheme to be used in the template
Purpose and the audience of the presentation
Number of slides to be shown on the day

questions.question_text: A presenter has to present a project to senior managers who have only ten minutes. The most appropriate approach is to:
options: Lead with the conclusion and recommendation and support it briefly
Spend most of the time on the methodology of the study
Show all the data collected, leaving the managers to draw their conclusions
Begin with the history of the subject and go through every detail

questions.question_text: A presentation to a technical audience of engineers differs from one to the board of directors in that the former can:
options: Leave out the data and graphs
Include more technical detail and terminology
Skip the conclusion
Avoid explaining the method used

questions.question_text: A typical structure for a project presentation is:
options: Introduction, objectives, method, findings, conclusion and recommendations
Conclusion, thanks, findings, method, introduction and objectives
Method, anecdotes, thanks, objectives, apology and the conclusion
Findings, apology, objectives, thanks, conclusion and recommendations

questions.question_text: The "objective" slide in a project presentation should:
options: Show the full text of the report
State clearly what the project set out to achieve
List the names of all the team members' families
Describe the weather on the day of the study

questions.question_text: The best number of key messages for a short presentation is generally:
options: As many as the speaker can recall
Twenty-five
Fifteen or more
Three or fewer

questions.question_text: A general guideline for slides is that each slide should carry:
options: The complete speech of the presenter
A different idea in each corner
One main idea with limited text
Several paragraphs of text copied from the report

questions.question_text: A commonly suggested minimum font size for readable slides is about:
options: 12 points for body text
24 points for body text
8 points for body text
10 points for body text

questions.question_text: The "6x6 rule" for slides suggests:
options: Six slides for every six minutes of the speaking time
Six colours with six fonts used consistently in a deck
No more than six bullet points with no more than six words each
Six speakers with six slides each in a team presentation

questions.question_text: Which slide design helps the audience read most easily?
options: Yellow text on a white background for a bright look
Dark text on a light background, or the reverse, with strong contrast
Light grey text on a white background for a soft look
Red text on a green background to attract attention

questions.question_text: For showing the change in sales over five years, the most suitable chart is a:
options: Table with no heading
Pie chart
Line chart
Scatter plot with no axes

questions.question_text: For showing the share of each product in total sales in one year, the most suitable chart is a:
options: Histogram of ages
Line chart over five years
Scatter plot of prices
Pie chart or a stacked bar

questions.question_text: For comparing the sales of five regions in one year, the most suitable chart is a:
options: Bar chart
Pie chart with thirty slices
Line chart with a single point
Radar chart with no labels

questions.question_text: A chart in a presentation should always have:
options: The raw data table printed in small type below it
3D effects that make every chart look attractive
A clear title, labelled axes and a legend where needed
Only decorative colours chosen to match the company logo

questions.question_text: A pie chart is a poor choice when:
options: The audience wants to see the share of each part
There are many small categories that are hard to compare
There are only two or three categories to be compared
The parts of the chart add up to 100 per cent

questions.question_text: A "call to action" at the end of a presentation tells the audience:
options: The list of the references
The name of the presenter
What you want them to do next
The time of the next break

questions.question_text: The best way to handle a slide with a complex diagram is to:
options: Read each label aloud without explaining
Show it in small print
Build it step by step so that the audience can follow
Show it for two seconds

questions.question_text: Reading the slides word for word is a poor practice because it:
options: Makes the audience read ahead and lose interest in the speaker
Reduces the time available for the speaker to talk
Helps the audience to follow the written text easily
Shows that the speaker knows the content thoroughly

questions.question_text: Visual aids should be used mainly to:
options: Display as much data as possible
Support and clarify the speaker's message
Replace the speaker altogether
Distract the audience while the speaker rests

questions.question_text: Using too many animations and sound effects in a presentation can:
options: Distract the audience and weaken the message
Help the audience to remember all the points
Reduce the chances of any error
Strengthen every message

questions.question_text: Which of the following is an advisable practice for using images on slides?
options: Use high-quality images that are relevant to the point
Use unrelated images to entertain the audience
Use as many images as can fit in a slide
Use blurry images to save the file size

questions.question_text: If you are presenting a project to a client, the title slide should contain:
options: The names of the competitors
The full list of the project expenses
The project title, presenter's name, organisation and date
The details of the personal life of the presenter

questions.question_text: An "executive summary" slide gives:
options: The full list of references used in the study
The project budget in complete detail
The raw data collected in the survey
A brief overview of the project and its main conclusion

questions.question_text: A project presentation typically ends with:
options: A summary of key points, recommendations and an invitation for questions
A blank slide to indicate the end of the session
A new topic that was not covered in the main part
An apology for the time taken by the presentation

questions.question_text: The best way to start a presentation is to:
options: Begin with a long personal story unrelated to the topic
Start reading the first slide without any greeting
Begin by saying that you are nervous and may make mistakes
Greet the audience, introduce yourself and the topic, and say why it matters

questions.question_text: Which of the following techniques helps to control nervousness before a presentation?
options: Drinking several cups of coffee beforehand
Rehearsing aloud and practising deep breathing
Reading the slides for the first time on the stage
Avoiding any practice before the presentation

questions.question_text: Rehearsing a presentation in front of a friend or a mirror helps to:
options: Remove the need for any slides
Improve timing, delivery and confidence
Make the presentation longer
Eliminate all questions from the audience

questions.question_text: A presenter who stands behind the lectern with arms folded and looks at the screen appears:
options: Confident and in full command of the audience
Disengaged, and may lose the audience's attention
Respectful and professional to the audience
Friendly and open to the audience

questions.question_text: Effective use of gestures in a presentation means that the gestures should be:
options: Constant and repeated regardless of the message
Natural and support the message
Wide and fast at all times
Avoided entirely

questions.question_text: The speaker's pace should be:
options: As fast as possible to cover everything
Uniform without a single pause
So slow that the audience loses interest
Moderate, with pauses to let key points sink in

questions.question_text: When the audience seems confused, the presenter should:
options: Tell the audience to read the report after the session
Ignore the confusion and move ahead with the next slide
Speed up to finish all the content in the given time
Pause, check understanding and restate the point more simply

questions.question_text: When you do not know the answer to a question from the audience, the best response is to:
options: Ignore the question completely
Admit honestly and offer to find out and revert
Blame the questioner for asking it
Make up an answer to avoid embarrassment

questions.question_text: A hostile question is asked by a member of the audience. The presenter should:
options: Argue back until the questioner withdraws the question
Raise the voice to dominate the room and the questioner
End the session at once and leave the stage
Stay calm, acknowledge the concern and answer with facts

questions.question_text: Before answering a question from a large audience, it is advisable to:
options: Repeat or paraphrase the question so that everyone hears it
Start answering at once in a low voice to save time
Skip it altogether if it is a long question
Ask the questioner to repeat it three times in a loud voice

questions.question_text: The part of a presentation devoted to taking the audience's queries is the:
options: Rehearsal session
Debriefing session
Briefing session
Question-and-answer (Q&A) session

questions.question_text: The word "Q&A" in the context of a presentation means:
options: Questions and Answers
Queries and Approvals
Quantity and Accuracy
Quality and Assurance

questions.question_text: A handout in a presentation is:
options: The full script of the speech to be read out by the presenter
The evaluation form to be filled in by the audience
A slide showing only the title and the name of the presenter
A document given to the audience with the key information or data

questions.question_text: The best time to distribute detailed handouts is generally:
options: In the middle, so that the audience may read during the talk
Never, since handouts are not useful in a presentation
After the presentation, so that the audience attends to the speaker
At the start, so that the audience may read ahead of the speaker

questions.question_text: A project report differs from a presentation in that the report is:
options: More detailed and written for reading at leisure
Shorter and meant to be spoken only to an audience
Always prepared in the form of slides and charts
Not required at all in the case of a project

questions.question_text: In a team presentation, the speakers should:
options: Avoid looking at one another to appear independent
Compete to speak the longest to impress the evaluators
Plan the order, rehearse the hand-overs and keep to their time
Speak together to show unity in front of the audience

questions.question_text: A smooth hand-over from one team member to the next is done by:
options: Reading out the next speaker's slide before he arrives
Saying nothing and walking away from the stage quickly
Summarising briefly and introducing the next speaker and topic
Interrupting the previous speaker as soon as the time is up

questions.question_text: If the projector fails in the middle of a presentation, the best approach is to:
options: Blame the organisers for the failure of the equipment
Cancel the presentation and ask for another day
Stand silently until the equipment is repaired
Stay calm, use a backup such as a printed copy and continue

questions.question_text: It is wise to reach the venue early in order to:
options: Test the equipment, slides and the sound
Avoid rehearsing
Skip the slides
Meet the audience for a long chat

questions.question_text: A backup copy of the presentation should be kept:
options: Only on the laptop
Only in memory
On a pen drive and in the cloud
Nowhere

questions.question_text: The time given for a presentation is 10 minutes. A suitable number of slides is about:
options: 8 to 10

questions.question_text: If your presentation overruns the time allotted, the audience is likely to:
options: Reward you for the additional effort made
Lose interest, and the organisers may ask you to stop
Appreciate the extra content that you have added
Not notice the extra time you have taken

questions.question_text: Citing sources on a slide or at the end of the presentation:
options: Is required only for the sources which are in print
Is a waste of time in a short presentation
Shows credibility and avoids plagiarism
Reduces the trust of the audience in the findings

questions.question_text: Using data from a competitor's confidential report in your presentation without permission is:
options: Smart research
Required
Unethical and may be illegal
A matter of style

questions.question_text: The most appropriate dress for presenting a project to clients is:
options: Casual beachwear
Formal or smart business attire
Party dress
Any torn clothing

questions.question_text: The audience of your presentation is a mix of experts and beginners. You should:
options: Explain key terms briefly and build up gradually
Use only technical terms
Speak only to the experts
Use only simple words and omit the data

questions.question_text: A storyboard used in preparing a presentation helps to:
options: Evaluate the presentation after the audience has left
Record the audio of the presentation for later use
Print the final slides in the form of a booklet
Plan the sequence and content of slides before designing them

questions.question_text: Mind mapping in planning a presentation helps to:
options: Choose the font and the colours of all the slides
Organise ideas and their links visually before choosing a structure
Time the speech of each member of the team exactly
Replace the slides with a single diagram on the board

questions.question_text: The "rule of three" in presentations suggests that:
options: Each slide should use three colours and three fonts
The speaker should use only three gestures
The presentation should not last more than three minutes
Grouping points in threes makes them easier to remember

questions.question_text: A "hook" at the start of a presentation is:
options: The list of contents shown to the audience on the first slide
An attention-grabbing opening such as a question, a fact or a story
The title slide with the logo and the name of the firm
The conclusion that is shown in advance to the audience

questions.question_text: "Tell them what you will tell them, tell them, then tell them what you told them" describes:
options: The method of conducting the question-and-answer session
A method of slide design using repeated slides
A way to confuse the audience with repeated points
The structure of an introduction, body and conclusion

questions.question_text: A "signpost" phrase in a presentation is, for example:
options: "Now let me move on to the findings."
"That is all I know."
"Please do not interrupt."
"Um, so..."

questions.question_text: When presenting numbers, the speaker should:
options: Round them and highlight the one or two figures that matter most
Read every number from the table in order to be precise
Skip the numbers and describe the trends in words alone
Use only fractions so that the audience can follow easily

questions.question_text: Which is the most effective way to express "profit rose from Rs 12,48,500 to Rs 15,01,200"?
options: "The profit has moved up somewhat since the last year."
"Profit is now higher than it was in the earlier year."
"Profit rose by about 20 per cent, from Rs 12.5 lakh to Rs 15 lakh."
"Rs 12,48,500 and Rs 15,01,200 are the two figures."

questions.question_text: The percentage increase from Rs 12.5 lakh to Rs 15 lakh is:
A bar chart shows that sales were 40 units in January and 60 units in February. The percentage growth is:
If the y-axis of a bar chart starts at 90 instead of 0 for bars of 92 and 95, the chart may:
options: Have no effect on how the bars are perceived
Reduce the visual difference between the bars
Remove the visual difference between the bars
Exaggerate the visual difference between the bars

questions.question_text: A presenter who uses a chart with a truncated axis to exaggerate a result is guilty of:
options: Using colour
Following the rule
Good design
Misleading the audience

questions.question_text: "Data storytelling" is the practice of:
options: Combining data, visuals and narrative to explain an insight
Reading out all the data from the table in sequence
Telling jokes about the data to keep the audience awake
Hiding the data that does not support the conclusion

questions.question_text: The most helpful title for a chart of monthly sales is:
options: "Sales"
"Sales rose steadily from January to June, peaking in June"
"Chart 1: Monthly sales for the first six months"
"Data for the first half of the year"

questions.question_text: In presenting a business proposal, the "benefits" section should:
options: Describe only the technical features of the proposal
Be skipped in a short presentation to save time
Show how the proposal helps the audience, preferably with numbers
Be kept for the end of the question and answer session

questions.question_text: "Features" versus "benefits": which statement expresses a benefit?
options: "This software will save your team ten hours a week."
"This software was developed in 2020."
"This software has a blue interface."
"This software has a cloud-based database."
questions.explanation: What it does for the user.

questions.question_text: In a business presentation, a SWOT slide would show:
options: Strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats
Staff, work, output and time
Sales, wages, orders and taxes
Schedule, workload, overheads and tasks

questions.question_text: A Gantt chart in a project presentation shows:
options: Profits against costs
Tasks against a timeline
Customers against products
Strengths against weaknesses

questions.question_text: A project timeline slide helps the audience to see:
options: The location of the offices of the team members
The names of the members of the audience present
The sequence of the activities and their deadlines
The total profit made by the firm during the year

questions.question_text: A risk matrix slide helps to show:
options: The marketing plan of the project
The likelihood and the impact of possible risks
The names of the employees of the project
The profits of each year of the project

questions.question_text: In the budget slide of a project, the presenter should show:
options: The salary of every employee working on the project
Every receipt and bill relating to the project
The major cost heads with their totals and the source of funding
Only the grand total without any break-up of the costs

questions.question_text: Return on investment (ROI) is computed as:
options: Profit multiplied by cost, expressed as a percentage
Sales divided by profit, expressed as a percentage
Cost divided by net benefit, expressed as a percentage
Net benefit divided by cost, expressed as a percentage

questions.question_text: A project costs Rs 5 lakh and gives a net benefit of Rs 1 lakh per year. The payback period is:
options: 1 year
0.2 years
10 years
5 years

questions.question_text: A project costs Rs 8 lakh and returns a net gain of Rs 2 lakh. The ROI is:
Milestones in a project plan are:
options: The names of the members who are leading the tasks
Key points of progress or achievement in the project
Distances between the offices of the team members
The rewards given to the team at the end of the project

questions.question_text: The stakeholders of a project include:
options: All the people or groups affected by or interested in it
Only the owners who have put the capital in the project
Only the staff who are working on the project
Only the customers who will use the final product

questions.question_text: The scope of a project defines:
options: What is and what is not included in the work to be done
The profits that the project is expected to earn
The names of the team members who will do the work
The order in which the speakers will present the project

questions.question_text: Deliverables of a project are:
options: The list of the risks identified at the start
The tangible outputs or results to be handed over
The fonts and the layouts of the slides
The list of the members of the audience present

questions.question_text: Feedback on a presentation is most useful when it is:
options: Vague and critical of the presenter's personality
Specific, balanced and aimed at improvement
Only praise without any suggestion for change
Given a year after the presentation

questions.question_text: After a presentation, a speaker should:
options: Blame the audience if the response was poor
Forget the presentation as soon as it is over
Avoid asking for any feedback from the audience
Reflect on the feedback and note the areas for improvement

questions.question_text: The "elevator pitch" for a project should take about:
options: 1 hour
15 minutes
30 to 60 seconds
5 hours

questions.question_text: An effective elevator pitch includes:
options: Who you are, the problem, your solution and the benefit
Every detail of the project in the order it was done
Only the price at which the product will be sold
Your whole life history and the history of your firm

questions.question_text: A good problem statement in a project presentation:
options: Praises the project and the team that carried it out
Lists the results obtained by the team in the study
Describes the issue the project addresses and why it matters
Describes the members of the team and their roles

questions.question_text: A literature review in a project report summarises:
options: The names of the authors of the report only
The profits earned by the firm in earlier years
What earlier studies have said on the topic
The opinions of the speaker on the topic

questions.question_text: The sample size is mentioned in the presentation of a market survey so that the audience can:
options: Be impressed by the effort of the team
Reduce the data to be remembered
Count the number of the slides in advance
Judge the reliability of the findings

questions.question_text: A survey of only 20 people used to claim that "all customers in India prefer our product" is:
options: A random experiment that proves the preference
Too small a sample to support such a general claim
A perfectly adequate basis for such a claim
A census of all the customers of the product in India

questions.question_text: A questionnaire for a survey should contain:
options: Clear, unbiased and relevant questions
Complex jargon that shows the researcher's expertise
Offensive questions that provoke a strong response
Leading questions that guide the respondent to the answer

questions.question_text: A leading question in a survey is one that:
options: Suggests the answer that the researcher wants
Asks about the leaders of the organisation
Asks the respondent for his name and address
Is placed first in the questionnaire

questions.question_text: Which survey question is biased?
options: "What did you like most about our service?"
"What can we do to improve our service?"
"How would you rate our service on a scale from 1 to 5?"
"Don't you agree that our excellent service deserves five stars?"

questions.question_text: Primary data are those that are:
options: Taken from old records of the organisation
Taken from the newspapers and the periodicals
Taken from existing books and published reports
Collected first-hand by the researcher for the study

questions.question_text: Secondary data are:
options: Imaginary
Already collected by others and used by the researcher
Not useful
Collected through the researcher's own survey

questions.question_text: A pilot study is:
options: The final study carried out after the main one
A study conducted on airline pilots in a training centre
A study conducted without collecting any data at all
A small preliminary study to test the methods before the main study

questions.question_text: In the conclusion slide, you should:
options: Restate the main findings and the recommendations
Introduce fresh data that has not been discussed earlier
Repeat all the earlier slides in a shorter form
Apologise to the audience for the findings of the study

questions.question_text: Recommendations in a project should be:
options: Impossible to carry out so that no one blames the team
Vague and general so that no one can object
Specific, realistic and linked to the findings
Unrelated to the findings to show originality

questions.question_text: A "limitations" slide in a project presentation is used to:
options: Praise the study and the team that carried it out
Criticise the earlier studies done on the same topic
Hide the weaknesses of the study from the audience
State honestly what the study could not cover and its weaknesses

questions.question_text: A "Thank you" slide at the end should be accompanied by:
options: Another full set of slides on the same topic
Contact details and an invitation for questions
A blank screen and a long silence
A set of jokes to leave the audience in good humour

questions.question_text: Good eye contact in a presentation means:
options: Looking at the floor to keep the thoughts in order
Looking at one person only, such as the head of the panel
Looking at the screen throughout the presentation
Looking at different parts of the audience in turn while speaking

questions.question_text: Using the laser pointer or cursor effectively means:
options: Indicating the relevant part briefly without waving it around
Keeping it moving all the time to hold the audience's gaze
Using it to circle every word on each of the slides
Pointing it at the audience to draw their attention

questions.question_text: The best attitude of a presenter towards the audience is:
options: Superior and dismissive of the audience's doubts
Respectful, enthusiastic and audience-centred
Indifferent to the reaction of the audience
Nervous and apologetic about the content

questions.question_text: The primary measure of a successful project presentation is whether the audience:
options: Admired the dress and style of the speaker
Clapped for the longest time at the end of the talk
Understood the message and acted as intended
Remembered the colours used in the slides
